KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, Florida (CNN) -- So, what's harder, steering a space shuttle or out-machoing Tom Cruise on the set of "Top Gun"? Scott Altman is commander of the current space shuttle mission to upgrade the Hubble Space Telescope. Scott Altman laughs when he answers the question. "Flying a space shuttle is a little more challenging than what we did in the movie, although the flying was a lot of fun," said Altman, who knows more than a little about both. The retired Navy F-14 fighter pilot is the commander of the current space shuttle Atlantis mission to repair and upgrade the Hubble Space Telescope. He also doubled for the actors, including Cruise, during the Southern California shoot of the 1986 hit movie. Then a young pilot, Altman had just gotten back from a 7½-month tour onboard an aircraft carrier when he got the "Top Gun" call from his commanding officer. "The skipper of our squadron picked four guys he thought he could trust to have this kind of carte blanche to break the rules a little bit," Altman said. That included a scene in which a brazen Navy pilot buzzes the base's control tower. That would never happen in real life, Altman said. The movie features Cruise as a young naval aviator, Pete "Maverick" Mitchell, selected to attend fighter-pilot training school at the then-Miramar Naval Station north of San Diego. To prepare for the film, Cruise flew in the backseat of an F-14 several times, including once with Altman. "The actors were all pretty easy to get along with. Tom Cruise, for example, was very motivated," recalled Altman, who is making his fourth trip into space this week. "He enjoyed flying. He listened to what we told him and became a pilot himself after that." Altman is not one to brag about his flying in "Top Gun." The U.S. space agency, NASA, doesn't mention his film heroics, either. But Altman is in one of the movie's most memorable scenes. While flying upside down, inverted, Altman gives an obscene gesture to the pilot of an enemy plane. "They said go ahead and gesture at the other airplane," said Altman, 49, with a smile. "So when you're looking at the scene where he's communicating with the Russian, or the bad-guy pilots in the movie, that would be my finger." But the flying scenes with the actors didn't all work out as director Tony Scott had hoped. "The director had to pay $7,600 an hour to rent an airplane," Altman recalled. "But after a week of spending that much money on the airplanes, he decided he couldn't use the footage. The actors all looked a little green, he said." Altman and the other pilots earned $23 a day for their trouble. But his biggest disappointment was not getting to see the film as soon as it was released. He and the other pilots were invited to a preview screening, but a commanding officer would not let them go. And by the time the movie hit theaters, Altman was busy. He was overseas, on another seven-month tour of duty.

**Title:** Beyond the Danger Zone: Why Flying a Space Shuttle Beats Hollywood Stunts

When moviegoers watched Maverick buzz the tower or flip upside down to give a MiG pilot "the bird" in the 1986 classic *Top Gun*, they were watching the work of real-life naval aviators pushing the limits of atmospheric flight. Among those elite pilots was Scott "Scooter" Altman, an F-14 Tomcat captain whose daring maneuvers provided the film with some of its most iconic aerial sequences. Yet, years after his brush with Hollywood stardom, Altman traded his fighter jet for a spacecraft, joining NASA and eventually commanding four Space Shuttle missions. Reflecting on both extraordinary careers, Altman came to a definitive conclusion: high-stakes Hollywood flying, as thrilling as it looks, pales in comparison to the immense challenge of steering a space shuttle.

To understand Altman’s perspective, one must first look at his time on the movie set. Flying an F-14 for *Top Gun* required instinct, lightning-fast reflexes, and a flair for the dramatic. Altman was the pilot who actually flew the roaring jet past the control tower and pushed the limits of tactical maneuvers to capture high-octane footage. In atmospheric dogfighting, a pilot relies heavily on immediate feedback—the roar of the engines, the push of high G-forces against the chest, and the tactile response of aerodynamic control surfaces biting into the air. If a Hollywood stunt didn’t look quite right, the director could simply call "cut" and order another take.

Spaceflight, however, operates under a vastly different—and far less forgiving—set of rules. 

When Altman transitioned to NASA, he found himself piloting a 100-ton spacecraft traveling at 17,500 miles per hour. In the vacuum of space, there is no air for wings to push against, no engine roar, and no atmospheric drag to slow you down. Instead of aerodynamic controls, maneuvering a shuttle relies on tiny Reaction Control System (RCS) thrusters. Every pulse of a thruster imparts momentum that will continue indefinitely until an equal and opposite burn is applied. 

Altman noted that while fighter piloting is a visceral, instinctual act, piloting a space shuttle is an exercise in supreme mathematical precision. During missions like STS-125—the final, highly dangerous servicing mission to the Hubble Space Telescope, which Altman commanded—there was zero margin for error. Aligning the shuttle’s robotic arm to grapple a multi-billion-dollar space telescope required maneuvering the massive orbiter within inches of its target while both objects zipped around the Earth at five miles per second. A single misplaced impulse from a thruster could cause a collision, destroying priceless scientific equipment or endangering the crew. 

The contrast became even starker during the landing phase. In an F-14, a pilot who misjudges an approach can slam the throttles forward, gain altitude, and try again. The Space Shuttle, by contrast, returned to Earth as a 100-ton unpowered glider. Dropping out of orbit at Mach 25, the shuttle had only one chance to land. Pilots referred to the orbiter’s landing characteristics as flying a "flying brick." Altman and his crew had to thread a precise thermal corridor through the atmosphere and align perfectly with a runway thousands of miles away, with no second chances and no engine power to save them if they came in short.

Ultimately, Scott Altman’s unique career highlights a profound truth about human flight. Hollywood can dazzle audiences with dramatic dogfights, high-G turns, and cinematic bravado, but the real pinnacle of aviation mastery happens quietly, thousands of miles above the Earth. Steering a space shuttle through the unforgiving geometry of orbit demonstrates that the extreme precision, cool-headed calculation, and absolute discipline required for real-world space exploration far surpasses even the most legendary feats of cinematic aviation.

Located on Florida’s sun-drenched Atlantic coast, the John F. **Kennedy Space Center** stands as a monumental testament to human curiosity, ambition, and technological triumph. For over six decades, this iconic facility has served as humanity’s primary launching pad to the cosmos, turning sci-fi dreams into historic reality.

The origin of the center is deeply intertwined with the dawn of the Space Race. Established in the early 1960s, it was named in honor of President John F. **Kennedy**, whose bold vision famously challenged the United States to land a man on the Moon before the decade was out. That audacious goal was realized in July 1969 when Apollo 11 lifted off from Launch Complex 39A. The thunderous roar of the Saturn V rocket carried Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, and Michael Collins into the history books, forever cementing the **center’s** role in human achievement.

Following the lunar missions, the **Kennedy Space Center** adapted to a new era of exploration with the Space Shuttle program. For thirty years, from 1981 to 2011, the center managed 135 shuttle missions. These re-usable winged spacecraft were instrumental in deploying revolutionary space observatories like the Hubble **Space** Telescope and constructing the International **Space** Station—a orbiting laboratory that remains a symbol of global cooperation.

Today, the **Kennedy Space Center** is experiencing a dynamic renaissance. No longer just a government facility, it has transformed into a bustling, multi-user **spaceport**. It serves as a bridge between NASA’s deep-space ambitions and the rapid growth of the commercial **space** industry. Historic launchpads are now leased to private pioneers like SpaceX, while NASA prepares its massive Space Launch System (SLS) for the Artemis program, which aims to return humans to the Moon and eventually pave the way to Mars.

Beyond its active launch sites, the **Kennedy Space Center** Visitor Complex serves as a powerful source of inspiration for millions of people each year. Standing beneath a real Saturn V rocket or gazing up at the flown Space Shuttle *Atlantis*, visitors of all ages are reminded of what humanity can accomplish when united by a grand vision. 

As we stand on the threshold of a new golden age of **space** exploration, the **Kennedy Space Center** remains the beating heart of our journey into the unknown—a place where history was made, and where the future is actively being launched.

Long before he became a veteran NASA astronaut and four-time spacefarer, the retired Navy captain was a real-life "Top Gun" pilot. And in the summer of 1985, he was the man in the cockpit doing the daring aerial stunts for Tom Cruise in the iconic film *Top Gun*.

For Altman, the path from the flight deck of an aircraft carrier to the commander's seat of Space Shuttle *Atlantis* was fueled by a singular passion for flight. But it is his brief stint as Cruise’s cinematic stand-in that remains one of the most legendary chapters of a decorated career.

### 'Negative, Ghostrider'

In 1985, Altman was a 26-year-old Navy lieutenant stationed at Naval Air Station Miramar in San Diego—the real-life home of the Navy Fighter Weapons School. When Paramount Pictures arrived to film a movie about elite fighter pilots, the Navy assigned Altman’s squadron, the VF-51 "Screaming Eagles," to perform the aerial sequences.

Altman, known by his call sign "Hooter," suddenly found himself strapped into an F-14 Tomcat performing maneuvers that violated almost every standard military protocol—with full permission.

Among his most famous cinematic feats was the iconic "tower buzz," where Cruise's character, Maverick, defiantly roars past an air traffic control tower, causing an officer to spill his coffee. 

"The director wanted us to fly low and fast past the tower," Altman recalled in later interviews. "We asked how low they wanted it, and they said, 'Oh, lower than that.' So we kept pushing it down until we were basically right at eye level with the tower."

Altman was also the pilot who flipped an F-14 upside down, hovering just feet above a "MiG-28" (actually an F-5 fighter) so his backseat officer could take a Polaroid photo of the enemy pilot—a scene that became an instant staple of 1980s pop culture.

"I used to joke that I did all of Tom Cruise's flying, but he got all the credit—and the paycheck," Altman said with a laugh.

### From Miramar to Orbit

While Hollywood gave Altman a taste of fame, his true ambitions lay higher than the stratosphere. 

The precision, discipline, and split-second decision-making required of a Navy test pilot—honed during his time at Miramar and aboard carriers in the Western Pacific—made him a prime candidate for NASA. In 1994, Altman was selected as an astronaut candidate, swapping his flight suit for a blue NASA jumpsuit.

His transition to spaceflight was seamless, but his *Top Gun* legacy followed him to Johnson Space Center. 

"When Scott arrived at NASA, everybody knew he was the guy who flew for Maverick," said a former colleague. "In a room full of the best pilots in the world, that instantly gave him ultimate cool points."

Altman logged his first spaceflight in 1998 as the pilot of STS-90 aboard Space Shuttle *Columbia*. He flew again in 2000 on STS-106, helping prepare the young International Space Station for its first permanent crew.

### Commanding Hubble's Rescue

Altman’s real-world piloting skills were put to the ultimate test when NASA named him commander of two of the most complex missions in space agency history: STS-109 in 2002 and STS-125 in 2009—the final two servicing missions to the Hubble Space Telescope.

 STS-125, Altman’s final spaceflight, was widely considered one of the most dangerous shuttle missions ever flown. Operating far from the safety of the space station, Altman commanded *Atlantis* as his crew performed five grueling spacewalks to repair the aging observatory.

Matching speeds with Hubble—orbiting Earth at 17,500 mph—and grappling it with the shuttle's robotic arm required the same nerves of steel Altman displayed decades earlier over the California desert. 

The mission was a resounding success, extending Hubble's life by decades and securing Altman's legacy as one of NASA's premier shuttle commanders. 

### A Legacy in the Clouds

Altman retired from NASA in 2010 after logging more than 40 days in space and over 7,000 flight hours in more than 40 types of aircraft. Today, he works as a senior executive in the aerospace industry, but he remains a revered figure in both the aviation and space communities.

Reflecting on a career that spanned the peak of naval aviation, Hollywood blockbusters, and the frontier of space exploration, Altman remains characteristically humble.

"I’ve been incredibly fortunate," Altman once said. "I got to fly the most amazing aircraft in the world, do things for a movie that pilots only dream of, and then command a spaceship to fix the window to the universe. You can't ask for a better ride than that."

To millions of moviegoers, Maverick was the ultimate pilot. But for those who know the real story, the man behind the stick was Scott "Hooter" Altman—a real-life hero who truly pushed the envelope, all the way to the stars.

In 1985, while stationed at Naval Air Station Miramar, Altman was one of an elite group of Navy fighter pilots tapped to perform the aerial stunts for a blockbuster movie that would define a generation: *Top Gun*. 

Now, decades after flying the iconic F-14 Tomcat as Tom Cruise’s stunt double, Altman is commanding the crew of Space Shuttle *Atlantis* on STS-125—a perilously complex, final human mission to repair and upgrade the Hubble Space Telescope.

### Flying for Hollywood

Before he ever applied to NASA, Altman was a top-tier aviator flying with the "Screaming Eagles" of VF-51. When Paramount Pictures arrived at Miramar to film *Top Gun*, the Navy volunteered Altman and his squadron to execute the heart-pounding dogfights and precision maneuvers seen on screen.

If you remember the iconic scene where an F-14 flies upside down just feet above a Soviet MiG, or the infamous moment where Maverick "buzzes the tower" against air traffic control's orders, you were watching Altman at the controls. 

"The director wanted a guy who could really handle the airplane," Altman recalled in a recent interview. "When we did the tower buzz, they told us, 'Fly low.' I asked how low, and they said, 'As low as you feel comfortable.' So I buzzed it pretty good. The tower control guy actually dropped his coffee."

Altman also famously provided the gloved hand flipping off the enemy pilot in the upside-down sequence—a moment that cemented the film's pop-culture legacy.

While Hollywood gave him a taste of fame, Altman’s ultimate dream lay beyond the atmosphere. Selected as a NASA astronaut candidate in 1994, he quickly traded his F-14 for the Space Shuttle simulator. 

Now a veteran of three previous spaceflights, Altman is back at the helm for what NASA officials are calling one of the most dangerous and technically challenging shuttle missions in history. STS-125 is the fifth and final servicing mission to the Hubble Space Telescope.

"In *Top Gun*, if you mess up a shot, the director yells 'Cut!' and you do another take," Altman said at a pre-launch press briefing. "Up here, there are no second takes. You have to get it right the first time."

Unlike missions to the International Space Station (ISS), the Hubble repair mission offers no safety net. Hubble orbits roughly 350 miles above Earth—much higher than the ISS—and in a completely different orbital inclination.

The crew is tasked with installing two brand-new instruments: the Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3) and the Cosmic Origins Spectrograph (COS). They will also perform unprecedented on-orbit repairs to damaged electronics, replace failing gyroscopes, and install fresh batteries intended to keep Hubble operational through at least 2014.

For Altman, who previously piloted the STS-109 Hubble servicing mission in 2002, returning to the telescope feels like visiting an old friend. 

"Hubble has rewritten the astronomy textbooks," Altman said. "To be the guy taking the team up there to give it one last tune-up, to extend its vision deeper into the universe than ever before... that’s a rush that eclipses anything you can do in a fighter jet."

"In space, especially on a mission like Hubble, every single move is rehearsed a thousand times. But when you’re sitting in the Commander's seat, watching that giant telescope drift into the shuttle bay, that same hyper-focus you learned in the cockpit takes over."

At Kennedy Space Center, where engineers and technicians still talk about STS-125 in hushed, reverent tones, Altman is remembered not just for his flying precision, but for his calm, steady leadership. He brought a touch of naval aviation swagger to the hyper-disciplined halls of NASA, keeping his crew relaxed through months of intense training and a mission fraught with tension.

The repair was a triumph. The instruments Altman’s team installed allowed Hubble to peer deeper into the cosmos than ever before, capturing images of the birth of stars and the collision of galaxies, unlocking secrets of dark energy, and inspiring a new generation of stargazers.

As the sunset turned the Florida sky into a canvas of deep violet and orange, Altman looked up.

"In *Top Gun*, we were playing at pushing the envelope for the movies," Altman said quietly. "But with Hubble, we were actually expanding the edge of human knowledge. To go from flying upside down over a jet in California to holding the universe’s window to the stars in the palm of our hand... you couldn't write a better script than that."

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a news feature comparing steering a space shuttle to flying fighter jets in Hollywood movies, featuring quotes from retired Navy pilot and astronaut Scott Altman.
counterfactuals.output:
**HOUSTON —** In Hollywood blockbusters, fighter pilots yank back on the control stick, slam the afterburners, and execute impossibly tight turns while yelling over crackling radios. It is high-octane, instinct-driven cinema—a world where raw adrenaline and brute engine power can solve any mid-air crisis.

Then there is the Space Shuttle. 

Entering the Earth’s atmosphere at Mach 25—roughly 17,500 miles per hour—the Shuttle did not scream through the sky with the roar of a jet engine. In fact, for the final 30 minutes of its flight, it had no engine power at all. It was a 100-ton, ultra-complex glider falling out of orbit.

Few people understand the stark contrast between movie-style dogfighting and maneuvering a spacecraft better than retired Navy Captain and NASA astronaut Scott "Scooter" Altman. 

Before he commanded two Space Shuttle missions—including the final, daring repair of the Hubble Space Telescope—Altman was a elite Navy test pilot. He was also the real-life aviator who flew the F-14 Tomcat for Tom Cruise’s stunt double in the iconic 1986 film *Top Gun*, even buzzing the control tower in the movie’s most famous flyby.

"In Hollywood, flying a fighter jet is all about spectacle, impulse, and noise," Altman says. "You see pilots pushing the throttle forward, pulling high Gs, doing inverted dives. If an approach looks bad, you just hit the afterburner, roar back into the sky, and try again. But in the Space Shuttle? You get one chance. There are no go-arounds."

### From Mach 2 to Mach 25

In movies, jet dogfights happen at supersonic speeds, but they are framed within a human scale. Audiences watch jets weave through canyons or dogfight at Mach 1 or 2, relying on quick reflexes and aerodynamic lift.

Steering a shuttle from space down to a Florida runway was a completely different beast, governed by atmospheric entry physics rather than tactical maneuvering.

"When you’re in orbit, you aren't flying in the conventional sense," Altman explains. "You’re using small RCS [Reaction Control System] thrusters—tiny puffs of gas—just to change your attitude in the vacuum of space. It’s quiet, precise, and unintuitive compared to a jet."

The real drama began at the Entry Interface, roughly 400,000 feet above the Earth. As the atmosphere thickened, the Shuttle transitioned from a spacecraft to an aircraft, enduring temperatures exceeding 3,000 degrees Fahrenheit as friction built up on its thermal tiles.

"In a jet, speed is something you control with your left hand on the throttle," says Altman. "In the Shuttle, gravity and drag are in charge. Your job is energy management. You’re constantly performing wide S-turns high over the ocean just to bleed off velocity so you don't disintegrate or overshoot the runway."

### "The Flying Brick" vs. The Sleek Jet

Hollywood loves to depict spacecraft flying like sleek fighter jets, darting through asteroid fields or making bank turns in atmospheric skies. But aerodynamically, the Space Shuttle had more in common with a lifting body than a agile jet. Pilots famously dubbed it the "Flying Brick."

Where a modern fighter jet like the F-14 or F/A-18 has a glide ratio that allows for forgiving landing patterns, the Shuttle plummeted at a steep 19-degree glide slope—more than six times steeper than a commercial airliner’s approach.

"In *Top Gun*, we made jet flying look like an art form driven by passion," Altman laughs. "In the Shuttle cockpit, as you hit the lower atmosphere, it was pure math and discipline. You’re dropping at 10,000 feet per minute. At 2,000 feet, you pull the nose up in a massive 'flare' maneuver to level out, drop the landing gear, and touch down. If you pull up too late, you crash. If you pull up too early, you stall and drop like a rock."

Furthermore, while movie pilots are constantly wrestling with the control stick, the Shuttle was largely flown by onboard flight computers during the intense heating phase of re-entry. The Commander typically took manual control of the stick only in the final minutes of flight, around Mach 1.

"Taking the stick of the Shuttle for the first time on re-entry is a feeling like no other," Altman recalls. "You move the hand controller, and this massive 200,000-pound vehicle responds. It doesn't snap into a roll like an F-14; it moves with a heavy, deliberate majesty. It’s not about lightning-fast reflexes; it’s about micro-adjustments and trust in your training."

### Cinema vs. Reality

Altman acknowledges that while Hollywood takes immense creative liberties with aviation—often exaggerating cockpit dialogue, alarms, and physics for dramatic effect—movies get one thing right: the sheer awe of flight.

"When people watch *Top Gun*, they fall in love with the romance of flying fast," Altman says. "And flying a fighter jet *is* a blast. It’s visceral. You feel the G-forces crushing your chest, you hear the wind, you smell the jet fuel."

"But looking out the overhead windows of the Space Shuttle, seeing the blue curve of the Earth set against the absolute blackness of space, and then guiding that machine all the way back down to a standstill on a strip of tarmac... there’s no movie magic in the world that can match that reality."

**CNN.com** | SPECIAL REPORT

# From Maverick’s Wings to Space Shuttle Commander: Astronaut Scott Altman recalls 'Top Gun' days ahead of fourth launch

**By Jason Carroll**  
**CNN**  

**(CNN) —** Long before he was preparing to blast into orbit at 17,500 miles per hour, Scott "Scooter" Altman was already living in the danger zone. 

To moviegoers around the world, he is the anonymous aviator who flipped an F-14 Tomcat upside down over a Russian MiG and famously buzzed the control tower in the 1986 blockbuster *Top Gun*. But to NASA, he is Captain Scott Altman: veteran test pilot, space shuttle commander, and one of the space agency's most trusted leaders.

Now, as Altman prepares for his fourth journey into space, the veteran astronaut is taking a moment to look back at the cinematic summer that helped define a generation of real-world aviators—and his own path to the stars.

"It’s funny to think about," Altman told CNN from NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, wearing his standard blue flight suit instead of the iconic leather jacket. "People watch that movie and see Tom Cruise, but when I watch it, I just remember the heat, the G-forces, and trying to figure out how to satisfy a Hollywood director without breaking any Navy regulations."

### 'Lower, Scooter, Lower!'

Altman was a young Navy lieutenant and elite F-14 pilot stationed at NAS Miramar in 1985 when Paramount Pictures arrived to film what would become one of the highest-grossing movies of the decade. Because of his exceptional piloting skills, Altman was selected as one of the key stunt flyers for the film. 

Working alongside the late director Tony Scott was, according to Altman, an experience almost as intense as spaceflight training. 

"Tony was a force of nature," Altman recalled with a smile. "He had this infectious energy. He didn't want CGI—he wanted real jets, real afterburners, and real sunlight cutting through the canopy. I remember flying the tower-buzz scene, and Tony kept coming over the radio saying, 'Lower, Scooter, lower!' At one point I thought, 'If I go any lower, I’m going to be walking into the control tower, not flying past it.'"

Altman credits Scott’s relentless pursuit of realism with capturing the authentic adrenaline of naval aviation, a visual style that inspired a generation of recruits—including future astronauts—to join the military.

### Training 'Maverick'

While Scott was orchestrating the chaos from the ground, Altman spent considerable time working directly with the film’s star, Tom Cruise. 

"Tom was incredibly driven," Altman said. "He didn't just want to pretend to be a pilot; he wanted to understand what makes a fighter pilot tick. He asked endless questions about the pressure, the split-second decision-making, the physical toll of pulling Gs."

Altman spent hours flying with Cruise in the backseat of the F-14, putting the actor through high-G maneuvers to get him accustomed to the aerial environment. 

"He handled it like a champ," Altman said. "You could tell even back then that he had a deep respect for aviation. It doesn't surprise me at all that he ended up becoming a licensed pilot in real life."

### The Ultimate High Altitude

While *Top Gun* sealed Altman's place in pop culture history, his ultimate dream lay even higher than the stratosphere. Selected by NASA as an astronaut candidate in 1994, Altman transitioned from naval aviation to space exploration.

Over the course of three previous missions, he has logged over 40 days in space, including commanding missions to the International Space Station and the Hubble Space Telescope. Now, preparing to strap into the space shuttle for his fourth and final spaceflight, Altman reflects on the stark contrast between piloting a fighter jet and commanding a rocket ship.

"In an F-14, you're maneuvering, you're reacting, you're feeling the air beneath your wings at Mach 2," Altman explained. "The shuttle is a completely different beast. Launching into space isn't flying—it's riding a controlled explosion. But the discipline, the focus, the trust in your team—that’s identical, whether you're over the Pacific in a Tomcat or orbiting the Earth."

As launch day approaches at Cape Canaveral, Altman acknowledges that the spirit of his *Top Gun* days remains with him. 

"Tony Scott taught me how to look at the sky with a sense of wonder, and Tom showed me what passion for your craft looks like," Altman said, looking out at the training mockups on the Houston hangar floor. "I’ve been blessed to fly the coolest hardware on—and off—the planet. But no matter how high I go, a part of me will always be that 26-year-old kid buzzing the tower."
